newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FEATURE - Singer's death exposes Nigeria AIDS time bomb.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singer's death exposes Nigeria AIDS time bomb.

text.p: The death of popular Nigerian musician Fela Anikulapo-Kuti from AIDS, a disease he refused to believe in, has exposed the risk of an exploding death toll in Africa's most populous country.
Other countries on the world's worst hit continent are making serious efforts to stop the disease spreading.
But in Nigeria the attitude has been one of at best complacency and at worst denial.
Doctors now hope that Fela's death will make Nigerians take the danger seriously.

"AIDS is spreading rapidly in our country...and when you start dying you will get the shock of your lives. Don't leave this place sniggering about Fela," the singer's doctor brother, Professor Olikoye Ransome-Kuti, told a gathering of his fans.
Anikulapo-Kuti, who created the Afro-beat sound and helped popularise African music around the globe, was 58 when he died.
He refused to acknowledge the existence of AIDS, which many of his fans called a "whiteman sickness", and reputedly slept with hundreds of women, refusing to use condoms.
Now he has become the best-known Nigerian to die of the disease.
NOBODY CAN RELY ON THE FIGURES.

Official figures on how many of Nigeria's more than 100 million people are infected with the HIV virus which causes AIDS are hard to come by. Based on small samples, their accuracy is doubtful and they are usually out of date.

"The last figure we had in 1996 for HIV infection was 3.8 percent of the sexually active population, that may be half or a quarter of the real level," haemotologist Professor Ibironke Akinsete told Reuters.
"These days we have an average of 10 to 20 patients a week in one hospital. Two years ago there were maybe two patients a week," she added.
In Africa, where homosexuality is frequently considered repulsive, AIDS is spread mostly through heterosexual contact.

Hushed silence among hundreds of fans, including many very frightened former girlfriends, greeted news of Fela's diagnosis. By the next day the news, and the fear, had crept onto the streets and into the workplace.
"I will definitely get an AIDS test now, this disease has really arrived here," said airport protocol officer Simon Okon.
AIDS IS JUST ONE MORE CRISIS IN NIGERIA
Fear and crisis are not new to military-ruled Nigeria, which has been in political and economic turmoil since the army annulled the 1993 election.

Despite its crude oil output, Nigeria's economy is deep in recession. Millions live below the poverty line in a struggle for daily life that leaves little time to think about AIDS, or even more visible killer diseases like malaria and diarrhoea.
The government has other priorities, and doctors say that only $300,000 per year is budgeted for AIDS prevention.
A senior naval officer suggested last year that infected women be sent to spread HIV among soldiers in neighbouring Cameroon, with which Nigeria has a border dispute.
"My information is that the government's efforts to prevent AIDS are abysmally inadequate, I believe the government is letting the people down," said Ransome-Kuti.
FELA'S DEATH COULD CHANGE PROMISCUOUS ATTITUDES
Doctors hope that the shock of Fela's death will make Nigerians change their behaviour.

"Fela's death should serve as a lever, especially for the youth. The impression I got when I saw Fela's fans was that many will say 'if such a person died of AIDS then it is time for a change of behaviour'," said Akinsete, who represents the Society for Women and AIDS in Africa.

The death from AIDS in 1989 of Franco, another great African musician, brought home the reality of the disease to the former Zaire. But it is not clear to what extent it changed sexual attitudes and behaviour in his anarchic and impoverished homeland.
In the West, it was the death of homosexual musician Freddy Mercury in 1991 that shocked many into awareness of the proximity of the disease.
"Until now many dismissed the AIDS issue with a wave of the hand, just as Fela himself had done on many occasions," said Thisday newspaper the day after the cause of Fela's death was revealed.
Ironically, some of Fela's closest followers are among those most reluctant to get the message. Some suggest he was killed by a slow poison injected by the drugs squad after a recent arrest.
"We all die somehow, Fela didn't die of AIDS, he just went to his ancestors because his time came," said one long-time friend of the musician at his club known as "The Shrine".
